title: Food
subtitle: spicy, bland, moreish; starters and side dishes
summary: Describe how food tastes and how well it is cooked, and handle a restaurant meal or a dinner at home with the right words.

lesson.heading: Flavours and tastes
rows: full of strong flavours, like a curry (opposite: mild)
with very little flavour - rather negative
with a lot of salt / a lot of sugar
pleasant, slightly salty or with herbs
sharp and not sweet, like a lemon; often unpleasant
with a good taste / with no flavour at all
so pleasant that you want to eat more

lesson.heading: Flavours in action
lesson.text: Notice how these adjectives behave: food *is* **bland**, but coffee *tastes* **bitter**. *Moreish* and *sickly* are especially common in speech.

examples.text: I love **spicy** food, especially curries - the hotter the better! My sister prefers **mild** curries.
Those cakes are too **sugary** for me. They have a **sickly** taste.
They had some delicious **savoury** snacks at the party. They were very **moreish**.
The coffee tasted **bitter** and the fruit juice was **sour**.
The food on the plane was **bland** and **tasteless** - it was like eating cardboard!

lesson.heading: Appearance, presentation and quality
lesson.text: These words let you complain politely - or praise - in a restaurant, and talk about eating well in general.

examples.text: This meat is **overcooked** (or **overdone**) / **undercooked** (or **underdone**).
I'm afraid this mango is a bit **unripe**. They're not really **in season** at the moment.
examples.note: unripe = not ready to eat (opposite: ripe); in season = being produced and available now

examples.text: This butter has **gone off**. I think we should throw it out.
examples.note: gone off = too old to be good to eat

examples.text: I don't feel like anything **heavy**. I just want something **light**; a salad would be fine.
British cooking can be very **stodgy**.
examples.note: stodgy = heavy and hard to digest

lesson.heading: Eating well - and badly
lesson.text: Talking about diet needs a small set of very frequent words.

examples.text: Zoe will only buy **organic** fruit and vegetables.
We should try to have a **balanced diet**, without too much or too little of any particular thing.
A diet of **junk food** can cause long-term health problems.
examples.note: junk food = unhealthy but easy and quick to eat

examples.text: **Processed food** in general is not good for you.
examples.note: processed = treated with chemicals to preserve it or give it extra colour or taste

lesson.heading: Eating out
lesson.text: At most good restaurants you have to **book a table** (or **make a reservation**) beforehand, and if you are ill you may need to **cancel the booking** (or **the reservation**). A meal in the UK is typically three courses.

examples.text: First a **starter**, then a **main course**, then a **dessert**.
examples.note: a starter is a light snack or appetiser

examples.text: You can often order **side dishes**, for example an extra bowl of chips.
examples.note: a side dish is a smaller dish served alongside the main course

examples.text: Some restaurants have a **set menu**, a selection of dishes at a fixed price; or you can order individual dishes, which is called ordering **à la carte**.
Restaurants often have **specials** advertised on a board.
examples.note: specials = dishes only available that day

examples.text: They often cater for **vegetarians**, **non-meat-eaters** and **vegans**.
examples.note: a non-meat-eater does not eat meat but is not a vegetarian; a vegan uses no animal products at all, such as eggs, cheese or leather

lesson.heading: On the table
rows: the cloth or paper square you put on your lap
one part of a meal, e.g. the starter or the main course

lesson.heading: Eating at home
lesson.text: A host offers food; the guest accepts. Learn these phrases as whole units - they are almost fixed.

examples.text: *Host:* Right, there's more soup. Who wants **seconds**? *Guest:* Oh, yes, please. It was absolutely delicious.
*Host:* There's bread here. Just **help yourself**.
*Host:* Be sure to keep a bit of room for some **pudding**.
examples.note: at home, dessert is often called pudding (uncountable), a sweet (countable) or afters (plural)

examples.text: *Host:* Can I re-fill your glass? **Say when**. *Guest:* **When!** That's fine. Thanks.

lesson.text: *Gone off* means food is too old to eat - it has nothing to do with leaving. Say *this milk has gone off*, not ~~this milk is old~~.

exercises.prompt: Which taste or flavour word describes each thing?

pairs.left: a pizza with cheese and herbs
a cup of tea with five spoonfuls of sugar
extremely strong black coffee with no sugar

exercises.prompt: The fish you ordered has obviously been cooked for far too long. You say: This fish is ___.
exercises.explanation: Food cooked too long is overcooked or overdone; food cooked too little is undercooked or underdone.

exercises.prompt: You ordered melon and it is very hard. You say: This melon is ___.
exercises.explanation: Unripe fruit is not yet ready to eat.

exercises.prompt: This piece of chicken is still pink in the middle. It's ___.
exercises.explanation: Undercooked or underdone food has not been cooked enough.

exercises.prompt: That pie was so heavy that I could hardly move afterwards. It was very ___.
exercises.explanation: Stodgy food is heavy and hard to digest.

exercises.prompt: You want to know whether the vegetables have been grown without artificial chemicals. You ask: Are these vegetables ___?
exercises.explanation: Organic food is grown without artificial chemicals.

exercises.prompt: Someone at your table recommends a big steak, but you just want a salad. What do you say?
options: I don't feel like anything heavy. I just want something light.
I don't feel like anything bland. I just want something sickly.
That steak has gone off. I just want something in season.
I don't feel like anything moreish. I just want something stodgy.
exercises.explanation: Heavy food fills you up; light food, like a salad, does not.

exercises.prompt: The peanuts were free and I just couldn't stop eating them - they were so ___.
exercises.explanation: Moreish food has such a pleasant taste that you want to go on eating it.

exercises.prompt: Match each restaurant word with its meaning.

pairs.right: a light dish before the main course
a smaller dish served alongside the main course
a selection of dishes at a fixed price
dishes only available on that day
someone who uses no animal products at all
someone who avoids meat but is not a vegetarian

exercises.prompt: It's a big student restaurant - you don't need to phone beforehand, so you don't need to ___ a table.
exercises.explanation: You book a table or make a reservation; if your plans change, you cancel the booking or the reservation.

exercises.prompt: Is each adjective a compliment about food or a complaint?

exercises.statement: If the butter has gone off, it means it has been taken off the menu.
exercises.explanation: Gone off means the food is too old to be good to eat: This butter has gone off - throw it out.

exercises.prompt: You are the host and you want your guests to serve themselves. Put the words in order.
exercises.answer: There's bread here. Just help yourselves.
exercises.explanation: *Help yourself* (or *yourselves* to more than one guest) invites people to take food without waiting.
